title: Ohm's law: V = IR
keyIdea: Resistance opposes the flow of current. It is measured in ohms (Ω). For a resistor at a steady temperature, the current is proportional to the potential difference (voltage) across it, and Ohm's law links the three: V = I × R, with V in volts, I in amps and R in ohms. Rearrange it to I = V ÷ R or R = V ÷ I. More resistance on the same cell means less current: 6 V across 3 Ω gives 2 A, across 6 Ω only 1 A. A longer or thinner wire has more resistance. On a graph of current against voltage, a resistor gives a straight line through the origin, and the steeper the line, the smaller the resistance. A filament lamp's line curves because its resistance rises as it heats up.
familyTip: Look at a phone charger or a lamp: the label gives the voltage, and sometimes the current. Use R = V ÷ I together to work out a resistance, and talk about why a long, thin extension lead gets warm when it carries a big current.

visual.caption: Does the current go up or down? Drag each card to a box, or tap the card and then a box.

Use a longer piece of wire

lab.caption: Flagship lab: swap resistors on a 6 V cell, plot I against V, rearrange V = IR, slide a clip along a wire and read resistance from slopes.

kid: Current is the flow of charge round a circuit. Resistance pushes back on that flow. We measure it in ohms, written Ω.
Put a bigger resistance on the same cell and less current flows. 6 V across 3 Ω gives 2 A. Across 6 Ω it gives only 1 A.
Ohm's law links the three: V = I × R. Volts equal amps times ohms. To find the current, do I = V ÷ R. To find the resistance, do R = V ÷ I.
A longer wire has more resistance. So does a thinner one. On a graph of current against voltage, a resistor makes a straight line. The steeper line has less resistance.
adult: Ages 12 to 13. The KS3 science programme of study for England includes current, potential difference and resistance, with resistance as the ratio of potential difference to current (R = V ÷ I). GCSE physics then uses V = IR in calculations and I–V graphs. It builds on measuring current with an ammeter and voltage with a voltmeter.

For a resistor at constant temperature, the current is directly proportional to the potential difference, so the I–V graph is a straight line through the origin; such parts are called ohmic. The resistance of a wire grows with its length and falls as it gets thicker. A filament lamp is not ohmic: as it heats up its resistance rises, so its I–V graph curves. R = V ÷ I still gives its resistance at any one point.

Common mistakes: thinking more resistance means more current; dividing the wrong way (R ÷ V instead of V ÷ R); multiplying when V is given; reading a steeper I–V line as more resistance; and mixing up the units, amps for current and ohms for resistance. Each one meets a resistor card, a triangle answer, a clip position or a line that will not fit.

practice.prompt: A current of {i} A flows through a {r} Ω resistor. What is the voltage across it, in volts?
practice.hint: V = I × R. Multiply the current by the resistance.

practice.prompt: A {=2*n} V cell drives a current through a 2 Ω resistor. What is the current, in amps?
practice.hint: I = V ÷ R. Divide the voltage by the resistance.

practice.prompt: A resistor has 12 V across it and 3 A through it. What is its resistance?
practice.hint: R = V ÷ I. Which number goes on top?
practice.explain: R = V ÷ I = 12 ÷ 3 = 4 Ω. 36 comes from multiplying, and 0.25 from dividing the wrong way.

practice.prompt: You swap a 3 Ω resistor for a 6 Ω one on the same cell. What happens to the current?
practice.hint: I = V ÷ R. The voltage stays the same. What happens when R doubles?
practice.explain: Doubling the resistance with the same voltage halves the current: 6 V ÷ 3 Ω = 2 A, but 6 V ÷ 6 Ω = 1 A.

practice.prompt: On a graph of current against voltage, line P is steeper than line Q. Which resistor has more resistance?
practice.hint: A steep line means lots of current for each volt.
practice.explain: Steep means more current per volt, which is less resistance. So Q, the gentler line, has more resistance.

pool.prompt: A {=5*n} Ω resistor has 0.2 A through it. What is the voltage across it, in volts?
A lamp has {=3*n} V across it and 3 A through it. What is its resistance, in ohms?
pool.hint: R = V ÷ I. Divide the voltage by the current.

pool.prompt: Which unit is resistance measured in?
pool.hint: Amps are for current and volts are for potential difference.
pool.explain: Resistance is measured in ohms, symbol Ω. Current is in amps and voltage is in volts.

pool.prompt: You use a wire twice as long, on the same cell. What happens to the current?
choices: It halves, because the resistance doubles
It doubles, because there is more wire
pool.hint: Does a longer wire have more or less resistance?
pool.explain: Twice the length gives twice the resistance, so with the same voltage the current halves.

pool.prompt: Why does the I–V graph of a filament lamp curve?
choices: Its resistance rises as it gets hotter
Its resistance falls as it gets hotter
pool.hint: The filament glows because it is very hot. What does heat do to its resistance?
pool.explain: As the filament heats up, its resistance rises, so each extra volt adds less current and the graph bends over.

pool.prompt: Maya works out I = R ÷ V = 3 ÷ 9 for a 9 V cell and a 3 Ω resistor. What went wrong?
choices: She divided the wrong way: I = V ÷ R = 3 A
pool.hint: In the triangle, V sits on top. What do you divide by?
pool.explain: Current is V ÷ R = 9 ÷ 3 = 3 A. Dividing R by V gives 0.33, which is the slip.

pool.prompt: A resistor gives a straight I–V line through the origin. What does that show?
pool.hint: Pick any two points. Is V ÷ I the same for both?
pool.explain: A straight line through 0 means I is proportional to V, so V ÷ I, the resistance, is the same at every point.

pool.prompt: Which change would increase the current through a wire on the same cell?
pool.explain: A thicker wire has less resistance, so more current flows. Longer or thinner wires have more resistance.
